Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is squaring off with President Trump, vowing to escalate a trade war between the two countries after negotiations spectacularly collapsed over the weekend.

   The whole “artificial” deadline was vintage Trump: Create a ticking clock that pressures your adversary to blink. So Trump created a deadline for imposing new tariffs on Canada. Canada didn’t agree to what the White House wanted on trade, and the tariffs went into effect after midnight Friday. 

   What exactly fell apart in the talks remains unclear (there is a ton of finger-pointing, and not a lot of commonly agreed upon facts).

   Regardless, Canada didn’t flinch. And this is becoming a theme.

   “You’re at war when you get attacked,” Carney told reporters , “and we got attacked.”

   At the beginning of 2025, countries (and companies!) were falling all over themselves to reach agreements with the White House. Trump claimed Japan, South Korea and the European Union all made agreements to invest gigantic sums of money in the U.S. in order to avoid tariffs (the details at the time were fuzzy).

   Countries aren’t buckling like that anymore.

   Trump has tried military threats and deadlines against Iran, and they are often ignored by Tehran. And, a number of times, Trump had backed off before launching the attack he said was looming. Then there was the Trump-announced peace deal between Israel and Hamas announced a few weeks ago that…neither side is abiding by.

   Being a lame-duck president is tough sledding. Some of Trump’s biggest priorities—creation of a White House ballroom , the Iran War and the trade war with Canada—aren’t things that Republicans are campaigning on in the midterm election. So he doesn’t have a lot of political cover or voter energy behind him at the moment. This weakens his leverage. He has shown time and again, though, that he believes he can create his own leverage. Other countries are watching, and voters are too.

Canada Digs In as More Countries Stand Up to Trump
 
Plus, the man bringing the Ten Commandments back into classrooms, and a look at how Warsh formed his views on inflation
 
 
KELLY CLARK/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Good morning. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is squaring off with President Trump, vowing to escalate a trade war between the two countries after negotiations spectacularly collapsed over the weekend.

 

The whole “artificial” deadline was vintage Trump: Create a ticking clock that pressures your adversary to blink. So Trump created a deadline for imposing new tariffs on Canada. Canada didn’t agree to what the White House wanted on trade, and the tariffs went into effect after midnight Friday. 

 

What exactly fell apart in the talks remains unclear (there is a ton of finger-pointing, and not a lot of commonly agreed upon facts).

 

Regardless, Canada didn’t flinch. And this is becoming a theme.

 

“You’re at war when you get attacked,” Carney told reporters, “and we got attacked.”

 

At the beginning of 2025, countries (and companies!) were falling all over themselves to reach agreements with the White House. Trump claimed Japan, South Korea and the European Union all made agreements to invest gigantic sums of money in the U.S. in order to avoid tariffs (the details at the time were fuzzy).

 

Countries aren’t buckling like that anymore.

 

Trump has tried military threats and deadlines against Iran, and they are often ignored by Tehran. And, a number of times, Trump had backed off before launching the attack he said was looming. Then there was the Trump-announced peace deal between Israel and Hamas announced a few weeks ago that…neither side is abiding by.

 

Being a lame-duck president is tough sledding. Some of Trump’s biggest priorities—creation of a White House ballroom, the Iran War and the trade war with Canada—aren’t things that Republicans are campaigning on in the midterm election. So he doesn’t have a lot of political cover or voter energy behind him at the moment. This weakens his leverage. He has shown time and again, though, that he believes he can create his own leverage. Other countries are watching, and voters are too.

What I’m Following

 
 
DESIREE RIOS for WSJ
 

The man driving a campaign to integrate religion into public education. David Barton, a former math and science teacher, has positioned himself as the intellectual architect of a movement advancing a conservative agenda in policy and education. Barton and his nonprofit have helped facilitate legislation in more than a dozen states to mandate the display of the Ten Commandments in classrooms.

 

How Kevin Warsh formed his views on inflation. Many on Wall Street applauded Kevin Warsh’s appointment as Federal Reserve chairman, seeing his record from 15 years ago as proof he is instinctively tough on inflation. But there is an alternative interpretation. Warsh might have a more unconventional view of what causes inflation, rooted less in demand-side indicators such as unemployment and more in the supply side and government policies.

A deal was reached that kept the company intact. Many DOJ officials regarded the political interference in the Live Nation case as extreme even for an administration in which the president has openly pressured law-enforcement officials to pursue perceived enemies and pardoned allies.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• By making inroads in some traditionally red states, Democrats have a chance to recapture the majority in the Senate.

 

• A Senate race in Iowa pits a Republican representative and former news anchor against a two-time basketball Paralympic gold medalist campaigning as a moderate Democrat.

 

• After chastising Trump for shredding U.S. climate policies, Europe, the U.K. and Canada are walking back their own environmental regulations.
